KPage: Cross-Block Page Compaction for Hardware-Efficient Sparse Attention

2026
Abstract.

Sparse attention reduces the algorithmic cost of long-sequence video Transformers, but three-dimensional token layouts can leave selected block-sparse regions only partially occupied. As a result, eliminating unselected blocks does not necessarily eliminate unused capacity inside the physical tiles that remain.

We present KPage, a page-compacted execution scheme for block-sparse attention. KPage decomposes selected K/V blocks into 16-row pages and packs valid pages across logical-block boundaries into large physical attention tiles. The packed tiles are assembled directly during K/V loading, without materializing an intermediate compacted tensor in high-bandwidth memory. KPage further routes partially occupied query blocks between M​64×N​256M64\times N256 and M​128×N​128M128\times N128 forward kernels, and uses exact score masking to preserve the original sparse-attention semantics. For backward, KPage constructs a K/V-owned paged layout and restores the original sparse adjacency after packing both Q and K/V.

Across five representative sparse-attention workload cases, KPage achieves 1.35×1.35\times–2.06×2.06\times bare forward-kernel speedup over NVIDIA Block-Sparse Attention (BSA), with a geometric mean of 1.77×1.77\times. On controlled workloads with fully occupied logical blocks, KPage is effectively on par with BSA (1.03×1.03\times geometric mean). Under matched-scale 3D layouts containing partial blocks, the geometric-mean speedup increases to 2.29×2.29\times. Execution-capacity analysis shows that Page16 K/V compaction and query-adaptive execution reduce physical query–key pair capacity from 334.1G to 177.5G positions while preserving 160.6G useful interactions. Across eight layouts reconstructed from the open-source Selective and Sliding Tile Attention (SSTA), Sliding Tile Attention (STA), and Video Sparse Attention (VSA) systems, the same KPage kernel has the lowest forward time in every case: 1.13–4.25×\times faster than the strongest exact baseline. The corresponding forward-plus-backward ratios are 1.02–2.71×\times. We further extend the metadata interface to independent Q/K partitions and evaluate the paper-matched Sparse VideoGen2 (SVG2) Wan 14B/720p configuration. KPage is 1.49×1.49\times faster than the strongest exact sparse baseline and 1.57×1.57\times faster than NVIDIA BSA. After compliance review, we will open-source KPage and submit a PR to NVIDIA cuDNN Frontend.

Keywords: 
Video Diffusion, Block-Sparse Attention, GPU Kernel Optimization, Long-Sequence Attention

1. Introduction

Self-attention is the core computation in Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017), and its quadratic complexity becomes particularly expensive in modern video diffusion Transformers (DiTs) (Peebles and Xie, 2023). State-of-the-art video generators typically operate on compressed spatiotemporal representations and use Transformer backbones over long token sequences  (Blattmann et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025b; Kong and others, 2024; Wan Team, 2025). In particular, modern video variational autoencoders (VAEs) compress video along both temporal and spatial dimensions, producing an underlying three-dimensional token organization that can be written as T×H×WT\times H\times W. Once flattened for Transformer execution, these representations can contain tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, making attention one of the dominant costs of both training and inference.

Sparse attention is a natural way to reduce this cost. Earlier work established structured sparse attention for long sequences using strided, local, global, or mixed connectivity  (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020). For video generation, the spatial and temporal structure provides substantially stronger sparsity opportunities. Recent systems exploit either structured spatiotemporal locality or content-dependent sparse selection. Sparse VideoGen identifies spatial- and temporal-dominant attention heads  (Xi et al., 2025); STA converts 3D local attention into hardware-friendly tiles (Zhang et al., 2025c); VSA learns dynamic 3D block selection  (Zhang et al., 2025b); SVG2 uses semantic clustering and permutation to densify selected regions  (Yang et al., 2025a); and Radial Attention constructs a distance-dependent sparse pattern for long videos  (Li et al., 2025). SSTA further combines selective and sliding-tile attention in HunyuanVideo 1.5 (Tencent Hunyuan Foundation Model Team, 2025). Other recent systems, including SpargeAttention, VORTA, FPSAttention, and SPADE, likewise exploit structured or dynamic sparsity to reduce video attention cost  (Zhang et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).

Despite their different sparse-selection mechanisms, efficient implementations of these methods share an important property: sparse attention is eventually quantized into block- or tile-level GPU execution. This is necessary because reducing arithmetic work alone does not guarantee wall-clock speedup. Efficient attention kernels depend on sufficiently large matrix operations, regular memory movement, and fused online softmax. Consequently, sparse selection can identify useful interactions at a finer granularity than the tiles a GPU executes efficiently.

This mismatch is particularly important for three-dimensional video layouts. A logical sparse block is defined over a flattened token sequence, while token validity is inherited from the original T×H×WT\times H\times W geometry. If a temporal or spatial dimension is not aligned with the blocking geometry, boundary blocks contain fewer valid tokens than their nominal block size. Unlike one-dimensional sequence padding, which is commonly concentrated at the end of a sequence, multidimensional boundaries recur along temporal and spatial surfaces and their intersections. After flattening, partially occupied blocks can therefore appear repeatedly throughout the sequence.

This is not a hypothetical corner case. Existing video sparse-attention systems have independently encountered closely related forms of intra-block under-utilization. STA identifies mixed blocks, in which only part of a hardware tile belongs to the desired 2D or 3D attention window, and redesigns the sliding pattern so that executed tiles are predominantly fully dense or fully empty  (Zhang et al., 2025c). SVG2 observes the same granularity problem for dynamically sized semantic clusters: a useful 128×32128\times 32 attention region executed with a fixed 128×128128\times 128 sparse kernel requires 75% of the physical computation to be spent outside the useful region  (Yang et al., 2025a). VSA exposes the complementary hardware trade-off: smaller sparse blocks provide finer selection granularity, but reducing the block size lowers kernel throughput; its implementation therefore uses a 64×6464\times 64 block-sparse kernel and carefully balances sparsity against hardware efficiency  (Zhang et al., 2025b).

The difficulty is that simply shrinking the compute tile is not free. The evolution from FlashAttention to FlashAttention-2 (FA2), FlashAttention-3 (FA3), and FA4 has progressively increased the importance of hardware-aware tiling, asynchronous data movement, and deeply pipelined matrix operations  (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026). ThunderKittens similarly builds high-performance attention around regular tile abstractions and asynchronous pipelines  (Spector et al., 2024), while FlashInfer and FlexAttention retain block-structured execution to combine flexibility with high GPU efficiency (Ye et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025). Thus, smaller execution granularity can remove padding but can also give up the efficiency of large attention tiles.

Current systems address this tension in several ways. STA changes the sparse pattern so that mixed blocks disappear. SVG2 changes the compute geometry itself by supporting dynamically sized blocks. General block-sparse executors such as NVIDIA BSA retain a fixed block representation while accepting valid-length metadata so that padded K/V rows are excluded from the mathematical attention result (NVIDIA, 2026). For fixed-tile block-sparse execution, valid rows from different selected logical blocks remain uncombined, leaving physical tile capacity underutilized. Fine-grained sparse execution such as FG-Attn gathers selected K/V vectors into packed shared-memory tiles  (Durvasula et al., 2025), but its fine-grained units represent the attention sparsity pattern itself rather than invalid rows inside an already selected 3D sparse block.

We present KPage, which removes partial-block waste by packing data rather than shrinking the large compute tile. KPage keeps the original blk128 sparse graph but divides selected K/V blocks into 16-row pages. Valid Page16 regions from different logical blocks are compacted across block boundaries and gathered directly into the shared-memory stages of the attention kernel. No compacted K/V tensor is materialized in HBM. The resulting physical tile remains large enough for efficient Tensor Core execution while containing substantially less padding.

KPage also addresses partial occupancy on the query dimension. Query blocks with at most 64 valid rows use an M​64×N​256M64\times N256 path, while larger blocks use M​128×N​128M128\times N128; both geometries contain the same 16,384 query–key positions per physical tile. Invalid rows in partial pages are masked before the online-softmax row maximum, preserving exact attention semantics. For backward, KPage constructs a K/V-owned paged layout, derives reverse-Q neighborhoods for packed K/V tiles, and uses page-pair adjacency metadata to restore the original Q–K sparse graph after both sides have been physically packed.

The page abstraction does not require Q and K/V to share one logical partition. We expose separate per-head Q block sizes and K/V block sizes and offsets, allowing independently clustered layouts such as SVG2 to reuse the same page execution. Q clusters retain the Q64/Q128 routes, while independently sized K/V clusters are placed on Page16 boundaries.

Our evaluation shows that the gain is specifically associated with partial-block fragmentation rather than a generic advantage over the block-sparse baseline. When every logical block is fully occupied, KPage and NVIDIA BSA are effectively on par, with a 1.03×1.03\times geometric-mean forward speedup. Under matched-scale workloads containing 3D partial blocks, KPage achieves a 2.29×2.29\times geometric-mean forward speedup. Across five representative sparse-attention workload cases, KPage achieves a 1.77×1.77\times geometric-mean bare forward-kernel speedup over BSA. Page16 K/V compaction and query-adaptive execution reduce physical query–key pair capacity from 334.1G to 177.5G positions while preserving 160.6G useful interactions, increasing pair-capacity efficiency from 48.1% to 90.5%. On the paper-matched SVG2 Wan 14B/720p configuration, the independent-partition extension is 1.49×1.49\times faster than the strongest exact sparse baseline.

1.1. Summary of Contributions

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose KPage, which packs valid Page16 regions across logical K/V block boundaries directly into large attention tiles, without materializing an intermediate compacted tensor in HBM. Query-adaptive tiling reduces Q-side padding, while K/V-owned page packing preserves the sparse graph in backward execution.

  • •

    We extend the same execution scheme to independent Q/K partitions, supporting sparse layouts with different query and key/value block boundaries, including semantic clustering.

  • •

    Across five representative workloads, KPage achieves a 1.77×1.77\times geometric-mean forward speedup over NVIDIA BSA, and 2.29×2.29\times on controlled 3D partial-block layouts. Across eight open-source SSTA, STA, and VSA layouts, KPage is 1.131.13–4.25×4.25\times faster than the strongest exact sparse forward baseline. It further achieves 1.49×1.49\times on the SVG2 Wan 14B/720p configuration.

2. State of the Art

Recent video sparse-attention systems have made substantial progress in both sparse-pattern design and GPU execution. Sparse VideoGen exploits spatial–temporal sparsity in pretrained video diffusion models and combines the sparse pattern with layout transformation and customized sparse kernels (Xi et al., 2025). STA targets local 3D attention and redesigns token-wise sliding windows into hardware-aligned tiles; its ThunderKittens-based implementation reaches 58.79% model FLOPs utilization (MFU) and accelerates attention by 1.61.6–10×10\times over FA3 depending on the workload  (Zhang et al., 2025c; Spector et al., 2024; Shah et al., 2024). VSA performs dynamic selection over 3D video blocks and implements dedicated block-sparse forward and backward kernels, reaching more than 85% of the MFU of FA3 while substantially reducing attention time at high sparsity  (Zhang et al., 2025b). These results demonstrate that modern video sparse attention is already heavily co-designed with high-performance GPU kernels.

Other systems follow similar hardware-aware designs. Radial Attention constructs structured spatiotemporal sparse masks and executes them with FlashInfer for inference and an FA2-derived block-sparse kernel for training  (Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; MIT HAN Lab, 2024; Dao, 2024). HunyuanVideo 1.5 deploys SSTA through a dedicated flex-block-attention library built on ThunderKittens; the implementation supports STA, selective sparse attention, and their hybrid for both training and inference  (Tencent Hunyuan Foundation Model Team, 2025; Spector et al., 2024). SVG2 goes further by supporting dynamically sized sparse regions. It observes that semantic clustering can produce, for example, a 128×32128\times 32 useful region that would waste 75% of the computation if executed as a fixed 128×128128\times 128 block, and develops dynamic-block-size attention kernels following FlashAttention-style execution (Yang et al., 2025a). SVG2 reports up to 2.30×2.30\times and 1.89×1.89\times end-to-end speedup for HunyuanVideo and Wan on H100, respectively. Our SVG2 study in Section 4.6 instead isolates attention-kernel execution and is not a reproduction of those end-to-end results. Collectively, these systems show that the state of the art already includes sophisticated sparse layouts, specialized block-sparse kernels, asynchronous data movement, and variable execution geometries.

NVIDIA BSA represents the corresponding state of the art in general block-sparse execution (NVIDIA, 2026). Its CUTLASS DSL kernels consume per-query lists of selected K/V blocks and support explicit valid lengths for partially occupied K/V blocks in forward. Thus, partial blocks can already be represented with exact mathematical semantics rather than treating padding as valid attention input. BSA nevertheless preserves the selected logical block as the unit of the sparse execution interface: valid rows from different logical blocks are not physically combined into the same K/V tile. The current blk128 backward path additionally requires full physical K/V blocks.

The above systems optimize different sources of sparse-attention inefficiency, but they do not target the particular padding studied in this work. STA removes mixed attention tiles created by the sliding-window mask by changing the sparse pattern itself. SVG2 removes padding caused by variable semantic-cluster sizes by varying the compute-block geometry. VSA studies the trade-off between sparse block size and kernel throughput. In contrast, our problem appears after a logical sparse block has already been selected: because valid tokens originate from a three-dimensional video layout, a selected blk128 block can contain substantially fewer than 128 valid rows. This layout-induced partial occupancy is independent of which sparse-selection algorithm produced the block.

Existing block-sparse kernels therefore leave a specific execution opportunity. A partially occupied selected block need not be executed as an independent under-filled physical tile if its valid subregions can be combined with valid subregions from other selected blocks. To the best of our knowledge, prior video sparse-attention kernels do not perform such cross-logical-block packing of valid sub-blocks while retaining a large physical attention tile.

KPage targets exactly this remaining inefficiency. It decomposes the valid K/V region of each selected blk128 block into Page16 units and packs pages from different logical blocks into the same physical K/V tile. The packed tile is assembled directly during K/V loading, without materializing a compacted K/V tensor in HBM. As a result, KPage retains the large Tensor Core execution geometry used by high-performance attention kernels while substantially increasing the occupancy of each physical tile. The sparse graph and its selection policy remain unchanged.

3. Methodology and Implementation

3.1. Overview

KPage retains the logical blk128 sparse graph while changing its mapping to physical attention tiles. In forward, selected K/V blocks are divided into 16-row pages and valid pages from different blocks are packed into the same large tile. Two query tile shapes reduce Q-side padding without merging Q blocks with different sparse neighborhoods.

Backward requires a different organization: multiple Q blocks may contribute to the gradients of the same K/V block. KPage therefore packs pages into K/V-owned tiles, traverses their reverse-Q neighborhoods, and records page-pair adjacency to preserve the original sparse graph. Algorithm 1 summarizes the execution flow.

3.2. Page-Granular Forward Execution

3.2.1. K/V page compaction

For logical K/V block bb, let cb∈[0,B]c_{b}\in[0,B] be its valid-row count and pbp_{b} its number of Page16 regions:

(1) pb=⌈cbP⌉,0≤P​pb−cb<P,p_{b}=\left\lceil\frac{c_{b}}{P}\right\rceil,\qquad 0\leq Pp_{b}-c_{b}<P,

where P=16P=16. Thus, the physical extent of a selected block decreases from 128 rows to 16​pb16p_{b} rows before final tile alignment. The remaining padding within each logical block is bounded by 15 rows.

For a query block qq, let 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} be the ordered list of logical K/V blocks selected by the sparse-attention algorithm. KPage expands these blocks into Page16 regions. Fully valid pages from all selected blocks are emitted first, followed by at most one partial tail page from each partially occupied block. Dummy pages are appended only when required by the physical iteration granularity.

This ordering serves two purposes. First, pages from different logical blocks can share a physical K/V tile, eliminating the requirement that each selected blk128 begin at a separate tile boundary. Second, the partial pages are confined to a suffix of the page walk. The kernel can therefore identify a prefix consisting entirely of valid rows and execute it without loading validity metadata.

The sparse graph is not changed by this transformation. A page is included only if its parent logical K/V block belongs to 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q}; KPage changes the physical packing of selected blocks, not the set of selected blocks.

3.2.2. Query-adaptive tile shapes

Page compaction reduces padding on K/V but does not reduce padding inside the Q block. Packing several Q blocks together would require merging their K/V neighborhoods, because different Q blocks generally have different sparse selections. KPage instead keeps every logical Q block independent and selects the physical tile shape from its valid-row count cqc_{q}, where MqM_{q} and NqN_{q} are the Q and K/V tile dimensions:

(2) (Mq,Nq)={(64,256),0<cq≤64,(128,128),64<cq≤128.(M_{q},N_{q})=\begin{cases}(64,256),&0<c_{q}\leq 64,\\ (128,128),&64<c_{q}\leq 128.\end{cases}

Empty Q blocks are skipped.

Both paths expose the same number of Q–K positions per physical tile: 64×256=128×128=16,38464\times 256=128\times 128=16{,}384. The Q64 path therefore reduces unused Q rows without reducing the tile area presented to Tensor Core. It consumes sixteen Page16 K/V regions per iteration; the Q128 path consumes eight.

The two optimizations operate independently. Page compaction reduces waste in the K/V dimension, while Q64/Q128 routing reduces waste in the Q dimension. Neither operation changes the sparse neighborhood of the query block.

Query blocks from the two paths are placed in separate persistent work queues. Within each route, longer page walks are scheduled earlier to reduce the tail caused by uneven sparse workloads. The underlying pipeline requires aligned iteration counts, so a small number of dummy pages can remain at the end of a walk. These pages are handled by the same validity mechanism as partial pages.

3.2.3. Direct page-guided K/V loading

Materializing the compacted K/V layout in HBM would require an additional gather kernel followed by another HBM read by the attention kernel. Instead, KPage uses the page table to assemble packed K/V tiles directly in shared memory during data loading, avoiding intermediate HBM materialization.

Each entry in the page table identifies a contiguous 16-row region in the original K/V tensors. An N​128N128 stage is assembled from eight such regions directly in shared memory. The Q64 path uses two adjacent N​128N128 page groups to construct its N​256N256 stage.

The shared-memory representation seen by the consumer is unchanged. After the producer has assembled a stage, the existing QK matrix multiply–accumulate (MMA), online-softmax, and PV MMA pipeline operates on a regular large tile. Page indirection is therefore confined to the producer side.

Fully occupied logical blocks also retain a regular access pattern. Likewise, backward detects aligned eight-page blocks and uses the original full-tile transfer path for them. Page-wise transfers are required only when physical tiles contain pages from different or partial logical blocks.

3.2.4. Exact handling of partial pages

A Page16 tail may contain fewer than 16 valid rows, and dummy pages introduced by alignment contain no valid rows. Zero-filling these rows is not sufficient for attention, because a zero key would still contribute a finite value to the softmax normalization.

KPage therefore masks invalid scores before the row maximum. Let Si​jS_{ij} and S~i​j\widetilde{S}_{ij} be the attention scores before and after masking, and let vjv_{j} indicate whether physical K/V row jj is valid:

(3) S~i​j={Si​j,vj=1,−∞,vj=0,\widetilde{S}_{ij}=\begin{cases}S_{ij},&v_{j}=1,\\ -\infty,&v_{j}=0,\end{cases}

This ordering is required for exact attention semantics. Since invalid scores are removed before the maximum and exponential, they contribute neither to the online-softmax maximum nor to its denominator.

KPage stores validity at Page16 granularity using compact bit masks. Two Page16 masks are packed into one 32-bit word. The page-table builder also records where the fully valid region ends, so validity metadata is only accessed for physical tiles that overlap the partial suffix.

The distinction is reflected in the kernel implementation. For fully valid tiles, KPage retains the fused score-loading and row-maximum path used by the underlying kernel. For a masked tile, the scores are loaded, the packed validity predicate is applied, and the row maximum is then computed from the masked values. The additional masking work is therefore restricted to tiles that actually contain partial or dummy rows.

For partial K/V pages, the unused suffix is also zeroed before the attention launch so that the Page16 TMA transfer remains a regular contiguous load. This zeroing is an implementation convenience; exact softmax semantics are provided by Eq. (3).

3.3. K/V-Owned Paged Backward

Forward page packing cannot be applied to backward without changing the work organization. In forward, a Q block owns one sparse walk and only reads K/V. In backward, several Q blocks can contribute to the same dK and dV rows. KPage therefore constructs a separate physical layout centered on K/V tiles.

3.3.1. K/V owner packing

A physical K/V owner contains eight Page16 slots. KPage allows pages from multiple partial logical blocks to share an owner, but does not allow one logical block to cross an owner boundary. If sbs_{b} is the starting page-slot index of block bb, the layout requires

(4) (sbmod8)+pb≤8.(s_{b}\bmod 8)+p_{b}\leq 8.

The constraint keeps all pages of one logical K/V block associated with the same physical owner. Its reverse-Q neighborhood therefore needs to be constructed only once for that owner.

Fully occupied blocks already contain eight pages and are kept aligned to a complete owner tile. Partial blocks are packed into the remaining owner tiles. This also provides a full-tile fast path: when the eight page identifiers correspond to one aligned logical block, the backward kernel uses the regular K/V tile load and store path rather than eight independent page transfers.

3.3.2. Reverse-Q construction and Q packing

A packed owner can contain pages from several logical K/V blocks. Backward must visit every Q block connected to any of these blocks.

Let ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} be the logical K/V blocks packed into owner tt, 𝒬⁡(b)\mathcal{Q}(b) the Q blocks connected to block bb, and 𝒢g\mathcal{G}_{g} a group of Q blocks. KPage visits their reverse neighborhood

(5) 𝒰t,g=𝒢g∩⋃b∈ℬt𝒬⁡(b).\mathcal{U}_{t,g}=\mathcal{G}_{g}\cap\bigcup_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\mathcal{Q}(b).

The grouping bounds the amount of serial Q work assigned to one backward work item for long sequences.

The reverse relation is constructed from the original Q-to-K sparse edges. KPage scatters these edges into an owner-indexed bitmap and then compacts the nonempty Q entries. This avoids constructing a separate K-to-Q edge array followed by a global sort.

Q data are subsequently represented at Page16 granularity as well. Full Q blocks remain aligned so they can use the regular 128-row load path. Pages from partial Q blocks are packed into the remaining physical Q steps. Thus, backward removes padding on both sides while retaining the 128×128128\times 128 MMA shape.

3.3.3. Restoring the sparse graph after packing

The reverse union introduces physical Q–K pairs that need not exist in the original sparse graph. For example, an owner may contain pages from two logical K/V blocks while a Q block is connected to only one of them. Executing the full Cartesian product of the packed pages would therefore introduce incorrect attention edges.

For a physical backward step, let qjq_{j} and kik_{i} denote the logical blocks owning Q-page jj and K/V-page ii, and let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the original sparse block graph. The page-pair adjacency is

(6) Aj​i=[(qj,ki)∈ℰ],A_{ji}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[(q_{j},k_{i})\in\mathcal{E}\right],

where 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function.

A physical step contains eight Q pages and eight K/V pages, so the complete 8×88\times 8 adjacency matrix requires 64 bits and is stored in one machine word. The kernel reads this word and masks page pairs with Aj​i=0A_{ji}=0 before reconstructing the attention probability. These pairs therefore produce zero probability and zero score gradient.

When all 64 page pairs are valid, the mask is represented by an all-valid value and the additional masking path is skipped. Packing therefore does not impose page-pair tests on regular full-tile cases.

The resulting dQ, dK, and dV fragments are written back through the existing FP32 accumulation and postprocessing layout. For mixed owner tiles, KPage scatters results by Page16 identifier; for aligned full tiles, it retains the regular bulk path.

3.4. Metadata Construction and Kernel Integration

The forward layout depends on the sparse graph and valid-row counts, not on the values of QQ, KK, or VV. The page table, Q64/Q128 route assignment, full-tile boundary, and suffix validity masks can therefore be reused while the sparse layout is unchanged.

Forward metadata construction scans the selected sparse edges to count the required Page16 regions, partitions active Q blocks into the two execution routes, and emits the page and validity tables. The generated metadata is consumed directly by the persistent forward kernels; no runtime K/V compaction buffer is allocated.

Backward metadata is constructed lazily because it is unnecessary for inference. The backward builder packs K/V owners, derives their reverse-Q neighborhoods, packs the corresponding Q pages, and emits the page-pair adjacency masks. The resulting layout can likewise be reused while the sparse graph and block occupancies remain unchanged.

KPage retains the large-tile arithmetic of the reference NVIDIA BSA implementation. Forward changes the K/V producer, introduces Q64/Q128 routing, and adds validity handling for the partial page suffix. Backward changes the physical ownership and traversal while retaining the 128×128128\times 128 attention-gradient computation. The sparse-selection algorithm and attention equations are unchanged.

3.4.1. Independent Q/K partitions

The shared blk128 layout used by the representative workloads is a special case of the page representation. More generally, for each head let cqQ∈[0,128]c_{q}^{Q}\in[0,128] denote the valid rows of logical Q block qq, and let (ckK,okK)(c_{k}^{K},o_{k}^{K}) denote the valid-row count and physical row offset of logical K/V block kk. We require okKo_{k}^{K} to be Page16 aligned and the page footprints of distinct K/V blocks to be disjoint. The sparse graph 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} indexes this K/V partition; the numbers and boundaries of Q and K/V blocks need not match. Clusters larger than 128 rows are represented by multiple logical blocks with the same sparse neighborhood.

Forward routing depends only on cqQc_{q}^{Q}, while the K/V walk emits page identifiers starting at okK/16o_{k}^{K}/16 and masks the final page according to ckKc_{k}^{K}. Backward independently packs the K/V partition and builds reverse-Q neighborhoods over the nQ×nK​Vn_{Q}\times n_{KV} sparse graph, where nQn_{Q} and nK​Vn_{KV} count the logical blocks in each partition. Padding-state cleanup likewise uses Q sizes for dQ and K/V sizes for dK and dV. The attention kernels consume the same page identifiers, validity masks, and page-pair adjacency words as in the shared case. The shared layout is recovered with nQ=nK​Vn_{Q}=n_{KV}, cbQ=cbKc_{b}^{Q}=c_{b}^{K}, and obK=128​bo_{b}^{K}=128b.

4. Experimental Results

4.1. Experimental Setup

We evaluate KPage using a controlled padding comparison and five representative sparse-attention workload cases covering varied sequence lengths, sparsity levels, and block-occupancy patterns.

Controlled workloads.

We construct two groups of matched-scale workloads corresponding to 5, 10, 15, and 30 s video sequences.

The first group contains no padding: all selected logical blocks are fully occupied. The second group uses three-dimensional layouts that produce partially occupied boundary blocks. Across these workloads, padding accounts for 20.8–22.8% of the physical sequence, and approximately one third of the logical blocks are partial.

Both groups use the same sparse-selection procedure and comparable sequence scales. Within each workload, KPage and NVIDIA BSA consume the same sparse block graph and the same valid-row metadata.

The two groups are not identical sparse graphs because the underlying layouts produce different numbers of logical blocks under the same selection procedure. We therefore use this experiment to compare two execution regimes: fully occupied blocks and layouts with substantial partial-block fragmentation.

Representative workload cases.

We additionally evaluate five sparse-attention workload cases spanning different sequence scales and sparsity regimes. Their physical sequence lengths range from 470K to 629K tokens, and their retained valid sparsity patterns vary across the cases, as do the proportions of partially occupied blocks. These cases evaluate page compaction across different sparse-attention settings.

The controlled and representative workloads use eight attention heads; the SVG2 traces use the model’s heads (12 for Wan 1.3B, 40 for Wan 14B). All workloads use head dimension 128 and BF16 inputs.

Baselines and software.

FA4 serves as the dense-attention reference in Figures 5 and 7, while NVIDIA BSA serves as the principal block-sparse baseline. The FA4-BSA column in Table 2 is a sparse kernel and must not be confused with dense FA4. For every reported forward comparison, KPage and BSA receive identical sparse metadata and valid-row information. Section 4.6 additionally evaluates layouts reconstructed from open-source SSTA, STA, and VSA systems. It compares KPage against NVIDIA BSA, FastVideo’s native and Triton VSA kernels, upstream FA4 block sparsity, and FlexAttention under the same GPU execution environment. It also evaluates the independent-partition extension on a trace from the official SVG2 Wan 14B/720p pipeline, including SVG2’s released variable-block kernel and the FA4-BSA path. The configuration matches SVG2’s published experiment, allowing its reported FA3-based results to be contrasted with the FA4-based measurements in our setup. These comparisons refer to different execution environments.

Experiments are conducted on a single GPU using CUDA 13.2. KPage is implemented with CUTLASS DSL, and NVIDIA BSA is provided by cuDNN Frontend 1.28.0. Since the generated BSA kernel can depend on the CUTLASS DSL version, we benchmark compatible BSA configurations using CUTLASS DSL 4.5.0 and 4.7.1 and report the faster result for each workload. The open-source layouts in Section 4.6 run KPage with CUTLASS DSL 4.4.2 and BSA and upstream FA4 (4.0.0b33) with CUTLASS DSL 4.7.1.

Timing methodology.

Unless otherwise stated, we report bare attention-kernel execution time. Sparse-graph construction, KPage page-table construction, Q64/Q128 route assignment, and backward layout construction are performed outside the timed region because these structures depend only on the sparse graph and block occupancies and can be reused while the layout remains unchanged.

The timed region contains the complete attention kernel, including page-table traversal, page-guided K/V loading, partial-page masking, online softmax, and output computation. No compacted K/V tensor is materialized in HBM.

For the controlled workloads in Table 1, we report the median of 20 timed iterations after 5 warmup iterations. For the five representative workload cases, we report the median of 10 timed iterations after 3 warmup iterations. For the SVG2 study, we report the median of 20 timed iterations after 3 warmup iterations. All measurements use synchronized wall-clock timing on a single GPU and a single execution stream.

4.2. Numerical Correctness

We validate KPage against an exact FP32 masked-attention reference. For each workload, we sample query rows from multiple heads and logical blocks and compare both forward outputs and backward gradients using the same sparse graph and valid-row metadata.

Across the evaluated workloads, KPage forward output errors remain in the same range as the BF16 BSA baseline, with maximum absolute errors on the order of 10−410^{-4}. The log-sum-exp (LSE) error remains below 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}. For backward, the cosine similarity of d​QdQ, d​KdK, and d​VdV is at least 0.99999 across the sampled cases.

These results confirm that page compaction changes only physical data placement and execution order; invalid rows and page pairs are excluded before softmax or probability reconstruction, preserving the original sparse-attention semantics.

For the independent SVG2 partitions, sampled forward outputs over all heads have relative ℓ2\ell_{2} error 2.34×10−32.34\times 10^{-3} (Wan 1.3B traces) and 2.35×10−32.35\times 10^{-3} (Wan 14B trace) against the FP32 masked reference, comparable to the released variable-block kernel’s 2.27×10−32.27\times 10^{-3} and 2.30×10−32.30\times 10^{-3}. A full-row backward check on one head of a Wan 1.3B trace gives relative ℓ2\ell_{2} errors of (2.37,2.35,2.32)×10−3(2.37,2.35,2.32)\times 10^{-3} for dQ, dK, and dV, respectively, against 1.66×10−31.66\times 10^{-3} for BF16 scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) on the same inputs.

4.3. Forward Performance

Table 1 compares KPage and NVIDIA BSA under fully occupied and 3D-partial layouts.

On the padding-free layouts, all logical blocks are full. The per-workload BSA/KPage speedups are 1.11×1.11\times, 1.03×1.03\times, 1.06×1.06\times, and 0.94×0.94\times, giving a geometric mean of 1.03×1.03\times. KPage and BSA are therefore effectively on par when page compaction is unnecessary.

This comparison also rules out a general kernel-speed advantage as the source of the padded-layout result. On these padding-free workloads, KPage’s pipeline alignment schedules approximately 1.4–1.5% more 128-row tile equivalents than BSA, while the measured performance remains close to parity.

Under the 2×8×82\times 8\times 8 3D layout, boundary cubes introduce 20.8–22.8% padding. KPage achieves 1.73×1.73\times, 2.20×2.20\times, 2.44×2.44\times, and 2.95×2.95\times speedup over BSA on the four workloads, respectively, with a geometric mean of 2.29×2.29\times.

The two layout families do not contain identical sparse graphs because their different block constructions produce different numbers of logical blocks under the fixed top-64 selector. The controlled result should therefore be interpreted as a comparison between two execution regimes: KPage is near parity with BSA when logical blocks are fully occupied, but provides a substantially larger advantage when the same selection procedure produces partial blocks under 3D boundary fragmentation.

We observe the same behavior across the five representative workload cases. KPage achieves per-case bare forward-kernel speedups of 1.90×1.90\times, 1.35×1.35\times, 1.94×1.94\times, 2.06×2.06\times, and 1.68×1.68\times over NVIDIA BSA, with a geometric mean of 1.77×1.77\times.

Figure 5 compares KPage with the ideal speedup derived from each case’s valid-pair sparsity. Based on the plotted values, KPage reaches approximately 76–79% of this ideal sparse-work bound, leaving approximately 1.26×1.26\times–1.32×1.32\times headroom.

4.4. Reduction of Padding-Induced Physical Work

We reconstruct the forward execution geometry directly from the complete q2k metadata and valid-row counts of the five representative workload cases. The useful sparse computation contains 160.611G valid query–key token pairs.

If every selected logical blk128 pair is represented by a full 128×128128\times 128 physical tile, the five workloads expose 334.109G physical query–key positions, corresponding to 48.1% useful-work utilization.

Page16 K/V compaction provides the largest reduction. Keeping the query side at M​128M128 while compacting selected K/V blocks at Page16 granularity reduces the physical pair capacity from 334.109G to 199.689G.

KPage additionally applies Q64/Q128 routing. Query blocks with at most 64 valid rows use the M​64×N​256M64\times N256 path instead of a full M​128M128 query tile. This further reduces the physical pair capacity from 199.689G to 177.548G, an additional 11.1% reduction relative to the M128-only paged layout.

Overall, this nominal packed-tile accounting reduces physical pair capacity by 46.9% relative to the whole-block layout and raises pair-capacity efficiency from 48.1% to 90.5%, while preserving the same 160.611G useful sparse interactions. The companion breakdown in Figure 6 also depicts residual union-mask and walk-tail overhead, yielding a slightly higher 180.3G total (89.1% useful) under that overhead-inclusive accounting.

These quantities characterize the physical capacity implied by the corresponding execution layouts. In particular, the 334.109G whole-block value should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of NVIDIA BSA forward FLOPs: BSA forward supports valid block-size metadata and preserves exact partial-block semantics. The direct BSA comparison is therefore given by the measured wall-clock results in Section 4.3.

The nominal accounting separates the contributions of the two forward mechanisms. Most of the reduction comes from Page16 K/V compaction, while Q64/Q128 routing removes a further 11.1% of nominal physical pair capacity by reducing Q-side padding. Figure 6 separately visualizes the additional overhead categories; its 180.3G total is therefore not the same accounting quantity as 177.5G.

4.5. Backward Performance

For training-oriented execution, we additionally measure the combined forward-and-backward bare-kernel time.

The padding-free workloads provide an exact comparison because every logical block is fully occupied and NVIDIA BSA backward does not require partial-block semantics. The per-workload forward–backward BSA/KPage ratios are 0.98×0.98\times, 0.98×0.98\times, 1.00×1.00\times, and 0.98×0.98\times, giving a geometric mean of 0.99×0.99\times. KPage and BSA are therefore effectively identical when no partial blocks are present.

Under the 3D-padded layouts, the corresponding timing ratios are 1.36×1.36\times, 1.33×1.33\times, 1.36×1.36\times, and 1.44×1.44\times, with a geometric mean of 1.37×1.37\times.

These 3D-padded backward numbers are reported only as a hardware timing reference. The current NVIDIA blk128 BSA backward path does not support variable block_sizes and therefore executes whole-block semantics on partial layouts. They should not be interpreted as an exact numerical comparison of the two backward operators.

Our primary quantitative comparison against NVIDIA BSA is therefore the forward result, where both implementations support the same valid-row semantics and execute the same sparse graph.

Figure 7 separately reports the five representative cases, normalizing forward-plus-backward kernel timings to dense FA4. These are distinct from the four controlled padding-length comparisons above; the BSA bars are timing references where partial-block backward semantics are not identical.

4.6. Generality Across Open-Source Sparse Layouts and Kernels

The preceding experiments cover several workload configurations. To test whether KPage generalizes to other video models and sparse selectors, we evaluate ten configurations from four open-source systems. The HunyuanVideo cases comprise SSTA at 480p and 720p with 121 or 241 frames, and STA at 720p with 117 frames  (Tencent Hunyuan Foundation Model Team, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c). The Wan cases comprise VSA at 480p and 720p with (4,4,4)(4,4,4) or (4,8,8)(4,8,8) spatiotemporal cubes  (Zhang et al., 2025b), plus SVG2 at 480p on Wan 1.3B and at 720p on Wan 14B (Yang et al., 2025a). SSTA combines a 3D window with top-kk selection, STA uses head-specific windows, VSA routes learned 3D cubes, and SVG2 independently clusters and permutes Q and K.

For SSTA, STA, and VSA, block occupancy follows the released geometry, padding rule, resolution, and frame count; we synthesize Q, K, and V because these quantities do not depend on sample content. For SVG2, we capture cluster sizes and selected cluster pairs from official end-to-end inference runs. Every case is converted to the exact block-index and valid-row metadata consumed by KPage; no kernel or schedule is specialized for a selector.

We compare with NVIDIA BSA (NVIDIA, 2026), FastVideo’s native CUDA and Triton VSA kernels (Zhang et al., 2025b), upstream FA4 block sparsity (Zadouri et al., 2026), FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2025), and SVG2’s released FlashInfer variable-block kernel (VBS) (Ye et al., 2025). On the 128-row-aligned SSTA, STA, and VSA layouts, BSA, VSA-CUDA, FA4, and FlexAttention run with 128-token blocks and VSA-Triton with 64-token blocks. On the SVG2 layouts, whose clusters are far smaller than 128 rows, each baseline uses its fastest exact configuration: 64-token blocks for VSA-CUDA, FlexAttention, and Triton, and 128-token blocks for BSA and FA4, which offer no smaller exact block. All runs use BF16, head dimension 128, and the same GPU. Metadata construction is excluded; each latency is the median of ten iterations after three warmups (twenty iterations for the SVG2 rows).

In Table 2, a VSA tuple (t,h,w)(t,h,w) is the temporal, latent-height, and latent-width cube. Pad is the invalid-row fraction after blk128 placement, and Partial is the fraction of nonempty blk128 blocks that are not full. For SVG2, which has independent partitions, Pad reports Q/K padding and Partial is marked indep.

On the eight shared-partition layouts in Table 2, padding ranges from 0.7% to 59.0% and the partial-block ratio from 5.9% to 100%. KPage has the lowest forward latency in all ten configurations. Relative to the fastest exact sparse baseline, the forward speedups are 1.221.22–1.46×1.46\times for SSTA, 1.13×1.13\times for STA, 1.241.24–4.25×4.25\times for VSA, and 1.491.49–1.93×1.93\times for SVG2. For the eight training-capable SSTA, STA, and VSA cases, KPage also has the lowest combined forward–backward time among exact baselines, with 1.021.02–2.71×2.71\times speedup. The nearly full-block STA case remains close to parity, while the largest gains occur when every selected block is partial.

SVG2 is the only special interface case. Its independent Q/K clusters require separate per-head Q sizes and K/V sizes and offsets; KPage places the K/V clusters on Page16 boundaries without changing the page kernels. The 1.3B/480p row aggregates 15 middle-layer traces with Cq=300C_{q}=300 and Ck=1000C_{k}=1000. The 14B/720p row matches the paper configuration (Cq=100C_{q}=100, Ck=500C_{k}=500, 30% dense warmup) on a released prompt; its 31.9% density is close to the reported 29.5–30.1%. The released SVG2 VBS interface exposes FA2/FA3 paths but does not provide a matching device-specific backend for our execution environment. It therefore uses FA2 and is slower than dense FA4 in our comparison. We report VBS alongside the compatible sparse kernels available in the same environment. SVG2 reports 2.98×2.98\times H100 attention speedup over FA3 and 1.60×1.60\times end-to-end speedup (1.89×1.89\times for SVG2-Turbo); our table reports attention-kernel latency and makes no end-to-end KPage claim.

All exact forward kernels match an FP32 masked-attention oracle to BF16 accuracy; training-capable kernels have gradient cosine similarity of at least 0.9999. The consistent ranking across these models, resolutions, selectors, and block geometries shows that the gain is not confined to the preceding workload configurations.

4.7. Summary

The controlled padding comparison shows that KPage remains near parity with NVIDIA BSA when every logical block is full, with a 1.03×1.03\times geometric-mean forward speedup. Under 3D-blocked workloads, where boundary cubes introduce 20.8–22.8% padding, the geometric-mean forward speedup is 2.29×2.29\times.

Across five representative workload cases, KPage achieves a 1.77×1.77\times geometric-mean bare forward-kernel speedup over NVIDIA BSA. Metadata-based execution accounting shows that Page16 K/V compaction reduces physical pair capacity from 334.1G to 199.7G pairs, while Q64/Q128 routing further reduces it to 177.5G. The resulting pair-capacity efficiency increases from 48.1% to 90.5% while preserving 160.6G useful sparse interactions.

These results show that KPage remains competitive when logical blocks are already fully occupied and substantially reduces the cost of partial-block fragmentation in three-dimensional video layouts. The same behavior holds on layouts reproduced from open-source systems (Section 4.6): against the fastest exact block-sparse kernel available for each layout, KPage has the lowest forward time in all eight SSTA, STA, and VSA cases. The geometric-mean forward ratios are 1.28×1.28\times for SSTA and 2.58×2.58\times for VSA; a nearly full-block STA case remains close to parity at 1.13×1.13\times. On the SVG2 Wan 1.3B middle-layer traces, KPage is 1.93×1.93\times faster than the strongest exact sparse baseline. On the paper-matched SVG2 Wan 14B/720p trace, KPage is 1.49×1.49\times faster than the strongest exact sparse baseline and 1.57×1.57\times faster than NVIDIA BSA. We do not infer a dense-FA4 speedup from the FA4-BSA column in Table 2.

5. Conclusion

KPage improves the execution of partially occupied block-sparse attention without changing the sparse graph or shrinking the large compute tile. It decomposes selected K/V blocks into Page16 regions, packs valid pages across logical-block boundaries, and assembles the resulting physical tiles directly during K/V loading. Query-adaptive M​64×N​256M64\times N256/M​128×N​128M128\times N128 execution reduces Q-side padding, while a K/V-owned paged layout extends the same compaction principle to exact backward execution.

KPage is effectively on par with NVIDIA BSA when all logical blocks are fully occupied (1.03×1.03\times geometric mean), but reaches 2.29×2.29\times geometric-mean forward speedup under 3D partial-block fragmentation and 1.77×1.77\times across five representative workload cases. Page16 K/V compaction and query routing reduce physical pair capacity from 334.1G to 177.5G positions for 160.6G useful interactions, increasing pair-capacity efficiency from 48.1% to 90.5%. The open-source cross-system evaluation confirms that this behavior is not pipeline-specific: across reconstructed SSTA, STA, and VSA layouts, KPage achieves 1.131.13–4.25×4.25\times forward speedup over the strongest exact baseline while remaining close to parity as blocks become full. Separate Q/K partition metadata further extends the same page kernels to SVG2’s independent semantic clusters. On the paper-matched Wan 14B/720p trace, KPage is 1.49×1.49\times faster than the strongest exact sparse baseline and 1.57×1.57\times faster than NVIDIA BSA.

The central result is that block-sparse attention need not choose between fine-grained padding removal and large-tile execution: fine-grained page packing can fill large physical tiles while preserving the original sparse-attention semantics.
